bridges.description: Infer that God exists from the combined permissibility of rational theistic belief and God’s comparative explanatory fit.
Establish that belief in God can arise rationally and non-inferentially under suitable experiential conditions.
Defend transcendent personal agency as a legitimate kind of philosophical explanation rather than a placeholder by definition.
Infer that a perfectly good personal creator better explains human access to objective moral facts.
Block evidential arguments from hiddenness, cosmic hostility, and apparently pointless suffering by challenging their theistic likelihood assumptions.
Infer that naturalism is preferable to classical theism and therefore that the God defined for the debate does not exist.
Give naturalism a pre-evidential advantage because classical theism makes additional specific claims.
Compare how expected the observed evidence is under naturalism and classical theism.
Use nonresistant unbelief and the value of conscious reciprocal relationship as evidence favoring naturalism.
Use cosmic hostility together with scale and apparently pointless suffering as evidence favoring naturalism.

sections.title: Rational belief and epistemic limits
sections.rationale: The opening dispute over proper basicality and its constraints bears directly on whether theistic experience can rationally support the motion.

sections.title: God as explanation and prior simplicity
sections.rationale: The parties distinguish whether God may explain anything from whether theism begins with a comparative simplicity disadvantage.

sections.title: Moral knowledge and disagreement
sections.rationale: Rauser’s sole positive evidential argument and Schieber’s principal replies concern the origin, reliability, and disagreement of moral cognition.

sections.title: Hiddenness and relationship
sections.rationale: The exchange tests whether nonresistant unbelief is unexpected if a perfectly loving God seeks conscious reciprocal relationship.

sections.title: Cosmic hostility and anthropocentrism
sections.rationale: The parties dispute whether a vast life-hostile cosmos is surprising under classical theism and whether that comparison assumes a human-centered creation.

sections.title: Suffering and unknown purposes
sections.rationale: The parties dispute whether apparently pointless suffering is comparatively expected and what finite knowledge permits observers to infer.

moves.speaker: Randal Rauser
moves.claim: Belief in God can be rational without inferential evidence when it is formed with the naturalness and immediacy characteristic of properly basic belief.
moves.warrant: Experiences reported as an immediate spiritual presence parallel other fallible yet prima facie rational belief-forming sources such as perception and belief in an external world.
moves.inference: Some theistic belief can therefore be rationally warranted apart from argument, although Rauser does not claim that it always is.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: This contiguous opening passage states the qualified thesis, defines properly basic belief, develops the external-world comparison, supplies the experiential example, and reaches the stated conclusion.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: one can have rational belief in god apart from evidence
moves.attributionRationale: The passage lies wholly within Rauser’s solo opening and maintains first-person argumentative continuity.
moves.importanceRationale: This is one of Rauser’s three announced pillars and establishes his route from experience to rational theistic belief.

burdenContact.rationale: It directly supplies the proposed non-inferential warrant for theistic belief.

moves.speaker: Randal Rauser
moves.claim: A transcendent personal agent is a legitimate philosophical kind of explanation and cannot be ruled out in principle.
moves.warrant: Philosophy already accepts transcendent explanations, and ordinary personal agency can explain events; combining transcendence and agency is not thereby non-explanatory.
moves.inference: God may properly be considered as an explanatory hypothesis when evidence is argued to call for such an explanation.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: The selected passage begins with the placeholder objection, defines transcendence, separates agency from transcendence, and ends with the limited conclusion that God is a legitimate explanatory concept.
moves.attributionRationale: This is a continuous portion of Rauser’s solo opening.
moves.importanceRationale: It clears a methodological obstacle but is expressly distinct from positive evidence that God exists.

burdenContact.rationale: It establishes the permissibility of personal transcendent explanation.

moves.speaker: Randal Rauser
moves.claim: God provides a better explanation of the human capacity to grasp objective moral facts than the naturalistic alternatives Rauser considers.
moves.warrant: Reductionism sacrifices objective moral information, Platonic realism leaves access to abstract goodness unexplained, while a morally perfect creator has the ability and motive to equip rational agents with moral knowledge.
moves.inference: Human moral cognition is positive evidence for a perfectly good personal creator.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: This passage introduces moral intuition as a cognitive faculty, develops the naturalistic explanatory challenge and alternatives, and states the theistic personal-agent explanation without relying on the later undeveloped list.
moves.attributionRationale: The passage is within Rauser’s uninterrupted opening.
moves.importanceRationale: Rauser identifies this as his positive test case for belief based on a feature of the world.

burdenContact.rationale: It supplies the positive evidential inference from moral knowledge to God.

moves.speaker: Justin Schieber
moves.claim: Naturalism is a simpler prior hypothesis than the specific classical theism defended in the debate.
moves.warrant: Basic naturalism and supernaturalism may be roughly comparable, but classical theism adds specific claims of omnipotence, omniscience, and perfect goodness.
moves.inference: All else equal, the simplicity difference gives a pre-evidential reason to prefer naturalism.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: This compact opening passage defines the comparison, distinguishes generic supernaturalism from classical theism, and states the limited pre-evidential conclusion.
moves.attributionRationale: It lies wholly within Schieber’s solo opening.
moves.importanceRationale: It sets Schieber’s prior comparison but is not offered as conclusive by itself.

burdenContact.rationale: It directly states the claimed prior simplicity advantage.

moves.speaker: Justin Schieber
moves.claim: The existence of nonresistant unbelievers is more expected on naturalism than on classical theism.
moves.warrant: A perfectly loving God would want meaningful conscious relationship with receptive creatures and would make belief possible for those who do not resist, whereas naturalism readily predicts the absence of God-directed evidence.
moves.inference: Nonresistant unbelief counts as comparative evidence for naturalism over theism.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: The passage defines genuine nonresistant unbelief, preserves Schieber’s conscious-relationship condition, lays out both likelihood comparisons, and states the evidential conclusion.
moves.attributionRationale: It occurs in Schieber’s uninterrupted opening.
moves.importanceRationale: This is the first of Schieber’s three central evidential observations.

burdenContact.rationale: It presents the full hiddenness comparison.

moves.speaker: Justin Schieber
moves.claim: The vast universe’s near-universal hostility to life, considered together with its scale, favors naturalism over theism.
moves.warrant: A universe created by a perfectly good God for embodied creatures could have been far more hospitable, while naturalism gives no reason to expect the universe to protect life.
moves.inference: The combined hostility-and-scale observation has a better evidential fit with naturalism.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: This is the complete argument from the pale-blue-dot setup through both comparative premises and conclusion, retaining Schieber’s qualification that size alone has little relevance.
moves.attributionRationale: It is within Schieber’s solo opening.
moves.importanceRationale: This is Schieber’s second principal evidential observation.

burdenContact.rationale: It supplies the comparative inference from hostility and scale.

moves.speaker: Justin Schieber
moves.claim: The massive amount of apparently pointless human and nonhuman suffering favors naturalism over theism.
moves.warrant: Schieber allows that some suffering may be needed for greater goods or to avoid worse harms, but argues that much moral and natural suffering appears unnecessary; naturalism predicts no protective concern for creaturely welfare.
moves.inference: The comparative likelihood of the observed suffering shifts support toward naturalism without claiming a logical contradiction.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: This passage explicitly distinguishes the evidential argument from the logical problem, preserves the allowance for justified suffering, covers moral and natural suffering, and includes the unknown-reasons symmetry qualification.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: the massive amounts of seemingly pointless suffering in the world strongly favor naturalism over theism
moves.attributionRationale: It lies within Schieber’s solo opening.
moves.importanceRationale: This is Schieber’s third central evidential observation.

burdenContact.rationale: It supplies the comparative suffering argument with its qualifications.

moves.speaker: Randal Rauser
moves.claim: Cosmic hostility is not clearly unlikely on theism because Schieber’s likelihood premise imports an anthropocentric expectation.
moves.warrant: Classical theism allows a creator whose work displays both immense grandeur and intimate detail; it need not make the whole universe a maximally comfortable human habitat.
moves.inference: The observed scale and severity do not by themselves establish Schieber’s claimed theistic surprise.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: The passage identifies the challenged premise, states the anthropocentrism objection, develops the architect analogy, and connects divine transcendence and immanence to the observed universe.
moves.attributionRationale: This is Rauser’s uninterrupted rebuttal.
moves.importanceRationale: It directly answers one of Schieber’s three principal evidential arguments.

burdenContact.rationale: It challenges the asserted likelihood under theism.

responseComponents.description: Challenges the anthropocentric expectation and offers grandeur plus intimacy as a competing theistic expectation.

moves.speaker: Randal Rauser
moves.claim: Finite observers are poorly positioned to infer that apparently pointless suffering is probably truly pointless.
moves.warrant: An apprentice may not understand a master’s purposes, and isolated hospital observations become intelligible only within a broader narrative of prior causes, later outcomes, and relationships.
moves.inference: Schieber’s first likelihood premise requires more contextual knowledge than humans possess.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: The full rebuttal develops both the apprentice and hospital analogies and states their shared epistemic reason rather than selecting only an illustrative fragment.
moves.attributionRationale: It is a continuous Rauser rebuttal passage.
moves.importanceRationale: It is Rauser’s principal reply to the suffering argument.

burdenContact.rationale: It contests the inference from apparent to probable pointlessness.

responseComponents.description: Argues that limited narrative knowledge undercuts the claimed theistic likelihood judgment.

moves.speaker: Randal Rauser
moves.claim: Meaningful relationship with God need not require explicit propositional belief that God exists.
moves.warrant: Rauser appeals to non-propositional parent-child relation and theological accounts in which people relate to God through goodness despite lacking correct concepts.
moves.inference: The presence of nonresistant unbelievers does not alone establish that a loving God has denied all meaningful relationship.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: This complete reply accepts that some nonresistant unbelievers exist, identifies the disputed conscious-belief assumption, and develops adult as well as infant examples.
moves.attributionRationale: This is within Rauser’s solo rebuttal.
moves.importanceRationale: It is Rauser’s primary rebuttal to divine hiddenness.

burdenContact.rationale: It challenges the claim that unbelief prevents meaningful divine relationship.

responseComponents.description: Disputes the necessity of explicit belief for meaningful relationship.

moves.speaker: Justin Schieber
moves.claim: Rauser needs a principled constraint that permits ordinary basic beliefs while preventing imaginative religious beliefs from gaining warrant too easily.
moves.warrant: The proposed method appears able to justify incompatible religions or fanciful entities; Schieber tentatively offers near-universal normal acceptance, ordinary direct formation, and the cost of denial as distinguishing criteria.
moves.inference: The analogy between belief in God and belief in an external world remains insufficiently defended.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: The passage states the permissiveness objection, explicitly denies equating God with fairies, introduces the three tentative universal-sanction criteria, and closes with the demand for a constraint.
moves.attributionRationale: It occurs in Schieber’s uninterrupted rebuttal.
moves.importanceRationale: It is Schieber’s main answer to Rauser’s first pillar.

burdenContact.rationale: It resists treating theistic experience as independently warranted evidence.

responseComponents.description: Challenges the proposed analogy as too permissive without a principled boundary.

moves.speaker: Justin Schieber
moves.claim: God can in principle serve as an explanatory hypothesis, but that concession supplies no reason that theism is actually true.
moves.warrant: A concept’s eligibility to explain is distinct from evidence that the concept gives the best actual explanation.
moves.inference: Rauser’s second point clears a conceptual objection but does not advance the motion without positive comparative support.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: This short passage contains Schieber’s explicit concession and immediately preserves its limitation before he turns to moral epistemology.
moves.attributionRationale: This is Schieber’s solo rebuttal.
moves.importanceRationale: It narrows what the explanatory-legitimacy argument accomplishes.

burdenContact.rationale: It insists that actual evidential fit, rather than mere eligibility, bears the motion.

responseComponents.description: Accepts the narrow conclusion while denying that it establishes truth.

moves.speaker: Justin Schieber
moves.claim: Moral intuitions may be prima facie justified without a presently known naturalistic mechanism.
moves.warrant: Immediate moral judgments may function like logical or grammatical intuitions: people can recognize a result while remaining unable to articulate the process, and such intuitions remain fallible and revisable.
moves.inference: Lack of a complete mechanism does not by itself make moral knowledge decisive evidence for God.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: The passage accurately identifies Rauser’s argument as moral epistemology, proposes the intuition comparison, and preserves fallibility and openness to revision.
moves.attributionRationale: It lies wholly in Schieber’s rebuttal.
moves.importanceRationale: It is Schieber’s direct alternative account of moral access.

burdenContact.rationale: It argues that naturalism can accommodate prima facie moral knowledge without a complete mechanism.

responseComponents.description: Offers a fallible intuition model and disputes the need for a known mechanism before justification.

moves.speaker: Justin Schieber
moves.claim: Persistent extreme moral disagreement is more surprising if God designed moral cognition for relationship and moral maturity than it is on naturalism.
moves.warrant: Theists occupy opposing sides of serious moral controversies; naturalism allows error and provides no guarantor of correct moral cognition.
moves.inference: The actual disagreement weakens the comparative force of the theistic moral-knowledge explanation.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: This self-contained segment asks the design question, states the observed disagreement, and contrasts the expectations of theism and naturalism.
moves.attributionRationale: The passage is in Schieber’s uninterrupted rebuttal.
moves.importanceRationale: It is a distinct empirical challenge to the reliability expected from divine design.

burdenContact.rationale: It presses a comparative evidential cost for the theistic design account.

responseComponents.description: Challenges the expected performance of a divinely designed moral faculty.

moves.speaker: Justin Schieber
moves.claim: Rauser’s appeal to cosmic grandeur does not answer the argument from hostility.
moves.warrant: A grand architectural work could still be expected to avoid pervasive lethal traps for intended occupants; Schieber did not require a small or maximally hospitable universe.
moves.inference: The life-hostility component remains unexplained even if the universe’s size is unsurprising.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: The passage grants that a large universe may display grandeur, then isolates and answers the distinct hostility issue with the house analogy.
moves.attributionRationale: It lies in Schieber’s solo rebuttal.
moves.importanceRationale: It directly preserves the key qualification in Schieber’s hostility argument.

burdenContact.rationale: It defends the hostility component against the anthropocentrism reply.

responseComponents.description: Concedes grandeur while arguing it leaves pervasive hostility unaddressed.

moves.speaker: Justin Schieber
moves.claim: Unknown divine reasons do not defeat a comparative evidential argument unless there is reason to expect unknown justifiers to outweigh unknown reasons for prevention.
moves.warrant: Possibilities beyond human understanding run in both directions, toward allowing and toward preventing hiddenness or suffering.
moves.inference: Mere appeal to mystery does not reverse the observed evidential comparison.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: This concise reply states both sides of the unknown-reasons symmetry and its exact limited consequence for the evidential argument.
moves.attributionRationale: It closes Schieber’s solo rebuttal.
moves.importanceRationale: It preserves Schieber’s answer to skeptical-theist reasoning.

burdenContact.rationale: It defends the likelihood comparison against an unsupported appeal to unknown purposes.

responseComponents.description: Argues that acknowledged ignorance is symmetric unless further evidence selects one direction.

moves.speaker: Randal Rauser
moves.claim: Epistemology may begin with naturally formed candidate instances of rational belief rather than a prior universal method.
moves.warrant: A particularist builds standards from ordinary instances, whereas Schieber’s method risks imposing a criterion chosen to include preferred beliefs and exclude others.
moves.inference: Failure to meet Schieber’s universal-sanction test does not by itself disqualify immediate theistic experience.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: This is the complete initial cross-examination setup before the mixed brief assent at E1824–E1825, so it preserves single-speaker ownership.
moves.attributionRationale: The first-person setup begins Rauser’s scheduled question; the mixed assent events are excluded from the span.
moves.importanceRationale: It identifies the deeper methodological disagreement behind the proper-basicality exchange.

burdenContact.rationale: It defends Rauser’s epistemic starting point against Schieber’s proposed criterion.

responseComponents.description: Challenges the demand for a prior method by defending particularism.

moves.speaker: Justin Schieber
moves.claim: Universal sanction requires acceptance by nearly all thinkers under normal conditions rather than literal unanimity.
moves.warrant: A small atypical group such as psychopaths does not defeat a criterion framed around normal belief formation, though Schieber treats the proposed line as plausible and open to improvement.
moves.inference: The criterion can retain ordinary moral belief while still constraining religious proper basicality.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: The passage begins Schieber’s answer to the psychopathy challenge and includes his explicit tentativeness and willingness that a better line may exist.
moves.attributionRationale: The turn follows Rauser’s question and uses first-person references to Schieber’s three criteria; contextual attribution is clear.
moves.importanceRationale: It answers a concrete objection to Schieber’s proposed constraint.

burdenContact.rationale: It defends the limiting criterion used against theistic proper basicality.

responseComponents.description: Clarifies that near-universal normal acceptance is qualified rather than exceptionless.

moves.speaker: Randal Rauser
moves.claim: An unprompted, immediate experience of spiritual presence can be a prima facie rational starting point even before a general criterion is settled.
moves.warrant: Rauser’s Burton Cummings example describes a surprising experience without prior religious preparation, and many people report analogous phenomenology.
moves.inference: Schieber has not shown why this kind of experience cannot initially ground belief in a spiritual reality.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: This passage states Rauser’s particularist alternative and returns to the concrete experiential case through the explicit conclusion about prima facie grounds.
moves.attributionRationale: First-person continuity and the return to Rauser’s own opening example identify the speaker in the scheduled exchange.
moves.importanceRationale: It applies the abstract particularist reply to the central experience example.

burdenContact.rationale: It argues that the experience itself can serve as a rational starting point.

responseComponents.description: Re-centers the dispute on a particular unprompted experience rather than a prior population criterion.

moves.speaker: Justin Schieber
moves.claim: Theism can be rational in some contexts without conceding that belief in God is properly basic.
moves.warrant: An experience may update a person’s prior probabilities, but evidential updating is distinct from non-inferential proper basicality.
moves.inference: Conditional rationality does not establish Rauser’s stronger classification of the belief-forming route.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: This exchange contains Schieber’s qualification, Rauser’s concession question, and Schieber’s final distinction and explicit statement that contextual theism can be rational.
moves.attributionRationale: The rapid exchange contains alternating short turns whose contextual ownership is intelligible but not independently audio-verified.
moves.audioVerificationReason: Verify the short alternating turns and the ownership of the final qualified concession before adjudication.
moves.importanceRationale: It preserves a crucial distinction that prevents overstating Schieber’s concession.

burdenContact.rationale: It limits what the experiential case establishes about non-inferential warrant.

responseComponents.description: Separates rational evidential updating from proper basicality.

moves.speaker: Randal Rauser
moves.claim: A nonbeliever’s pursuit of justice and mercy can constitute a substantial implicit relationship with God even without recognizing God.
moves.warrant: If divine goodness is expressed through justice and mercy, someone devoted to those goods may relate to God as a person can relate to water without knowing its chemical description.
moves.inference: Unbelief need not imply absence of morally meaningful divine relationship.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: This passage gives the adult aid-worker case in full, explains the justice-and-mercy relation, supplies the H2O analogy, and connects it to the cited theological interpretation.
moves.attributionRationale: The illustrative answer and first-person theological framing identify Rauser throughout.
moves.importanceRationale: It strengthens Rauser’s hiddenness reply beyond the infant analogy.

burdenContact.rationale: It proposes a substantive form of implicit relationship for a nonbeliever.

responseComponents.description: Supplies an adult case of meaningful relationship without explicit belief.

moves.speaker: Justin Schieber
moves.claim: Implicit orientation toward moral goods is thinner than the conscious reciprocal relationship a loving God would make available to receptive persons.
moves.warrant: Explicit friendship with a perfectly good being could deepen moral understanding and character beyond what an unrecognized relation supplies.
moves.inference: The possibility of implicit relation does not remove the evidential question why conscious relationship and its additional benefits are withheld.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: This immediate response grants a Christian tradition of implicit relation but states the distinct benefits and two-way character that motivate Schieber’s hiddenness premise.
moves.attributionRationale: The explicit reference to Schellenberg’s rationale and the responsive turn identify Schieber.
moves.importanceRationale: It preserves the conscious-reciprocal qualification central to the hiddenness argument.

burdenContact.rationale: It explains why implicit relation does not exhaust the good expected from divine love.

responseComponents.description: Grants implicit relation but distinguishes the additional benefits of explicit reciprocity.

moves.speaker: Randal Rauser
moves.claim: A loving God might temporarily remain hidden when immediate disclosure would provoke rejection and damage a person’s relationship.
moves.warrant: For an unbeliever whose suffering has produced protest, stepping back while the person continues to seek justice and mercy could preserve a route toward later reconciliation.
moves.inference: At least some nonresistant unbelief may be compatible with a loving God’s relational aims.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: This compact reply states the conditional scenario, the relational risk, and the limited possibility conclusion without generalizing it to all unbelievers.
moves.attributionRationale: It is Rauser’s direct continuation of his aid-worker illustration.
moves.importanceRationale: It offers a distinct possible reason for temporary hiddenness.

burdenContact.rationale: It supplies a relationally grounded compatibility response.

responseComponents.description: Suggests that immediate explicit relation can sometimes undermine rather than advance later relationship.

moves.speaker: Justin Schieber
moves.claim: Schieber does not know the naturalistic mechanism for moral intuition and allows that this particular fact might favor theism, while denying that mystery alone settles the whole case.
moves.warrant: Every worldview retains mysteries, and identifying one unanswered mechanism is relevant evidence but not an automatic demonstration of theism.
moves.inference: The moral-cognition datum may count locally for theism without conceding Rauser’s full comparative conclusion.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: This final scheduled exchange preserves Schieber’s explicit ignorance, his limited evidential concession, and the qualification that all views contain mysteries.
moves.attributionRationale: The alternating question and terse answer are contextually clear but rely on canonical captions without audio verification.
moves.audioVerificationReason: Verify ownership of Schieber’s short answer and limited concession before adjudication.
moves.importanceRationale: It is a material concession with an equally material limit.

burdenContact.rationale: It calibrates rather than abandons the comparative naturalist position.

responseComponents.description: Concedes possible local evidential weight while withholding the broader conclusion.

moves.speaker: Randal Rauser
moves.claim: Schieber has not adequately defended his methodological constraints, while the particularist experiential route remains available.
moves.warrant: The universal-sanction threshold is left unclear and risks pressure on ordinary moral knowledge, whereas an immediate experience such as Cummings’s can serve as a particular rational starting point.
moves.inference: Rauser’s qualified proper-basicality claim survives the rebuttal.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: This closing passage revisits the exact methodological dispute, the percentage problem, and the experiential conclusion without including unrelated later topics.
moves.attributionRationale: It is Rauser’s formal closing.
moves.importanceRationale: It is Rauser’s final answer on his first pillar.

burdenContact.rationale: It closes the dispute over methodological constraints and experience.

responseComponents.description: Defends particularism against the proposed prior constraint.
Presses the unresolved threshold for near-universal agreement.
Reasserts that the particular experience may ground proper basicality.

moves.speaker: Randal Rauser
moves.claim: Moral disagreement does not eliminate a broadly shared moral faculty or its need for explanation.
moves.warrant: Cultures share basic norms such as honoring parents and truth-telling, while human self-justification and fallenness can explain divergence from acknowledged standards.
moves.inference: Observed disagreement is compatible with significant moral knowledge and does not by itself defeat the theistic explanation.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: This closing segment restates the mechanism challenge, then directly answers the earlier disagreement objection with cross-cultural consensus and self-justification.
moves.attributionRationale: It lies in Rauser’s formal closing.
moves.importanceRationale: It supplies the late reply the source notes require retaining.

burdenContact.rationale: It defends the moral-cognition argument against its principal empirical objection.

responseComponents.description: Argues that labeling the faculty intuition does not explain its truth-directed capacity.
Appeals to basic consensus and human self-justification to explain disagreement.
Treats the admitted mechanism gap as continuing comparative evidence.

moves.speaker: Randal Rauser
moves.claim: Nonresistant unbelievers may still have meaningful non-propositional relationship with God through pursuit of justice.
moves.warrant: Biblical and broader theistic resources permit people to relate to divine goodness without explicitly identifying God.
moves.inference: Hiddenness does not establish the absence of all meaningful relationship.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: The closing passage briefly revisits cosmic hostility, then gives Rauser’s final hiddenness summary; the span ends before the non-argumentative dialogue appeal.
moves.attributionRationale: It is in Rauser’s formal closing.
moves.importanceRationale: It preserves Rauser’s final burden-specific hiddenness response.

burdenContact.rationale: It reiterates the implicit-relationship answer at closing.

responseComponents.description: Maintains that non-propositional relationship can still be meaningful.

moves.speaker: Justin Schieber
moves.claim: The permissiveness objection functions as a reductio: some limitation is needed even if Schieber’s proposed criterion is replaceable.
moves.warrant: Without a boundary, the same approach could in principle justify a great-pumpkin-type belief; Rauser did not articulate limiting conditions in the debate.
moves.inference: Rauser’s proper-basicality case remains incomplete even granting that some beliefs are properly basic.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: This closing passage accurately reframes Schieber’s earlier challenge as a reductio, grants common ground about basic beliefs, and states the unresolved need for limitations.
moves.attributionRationale: It is Schieber’s formal closing.
moves.importanceRationale: It is Schieber’s final formulation of his main epistemic objection.

burdenContact.rationale: It blocks treating the experiential route as established support for theism.

responseComponents.description: Recasts the objection as a demand for some boundary rather than exclusive commitment to one method.

moves.speaker: Justin Schieber
moves.claim: The morally valuable conduct of a nonbeliever does not supply the conscious explicit relationship expected from perfect divine love.
moves.warrant: A receptive creature could gain the best form of relationship and further moral benefit through conscious reciprocity, while the aid worker remains unaware of any divine partner.
moves.inference: Rauser’s implicit-relationship examples do not dissolve the hiddenness evidence.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: This closing segment preserves Schieber’s distinction between the morally good aid work and what he calls the thin or trivial relation to an unrecognized God.
moves.attributionRationale: It is Schieber’s formal closing.
moves.importanceRationale: It is the final direct response to Rauser’s hiddenness account.

burdenContact.rationale: It restores the conscious reciprocal relationship condition.

responseComponents.description: Argues that an open person’s best available relationship remains conscious and explicit.
Distinguishes good conduct from conscious relationship with God.

moves.speaker: Justin Schieber
moves.claim: The hostility argument requires neither anthropocentrism nor maximal hospitality.
moves.warrant: Schieber asks why nearly everything beyond the small habitable region is lethal, not why the whole universe was made exclusively for humans or perfectly safe.
moves.inference: Rauser’s anthropocentrism reply does not address the moderate comparative expectation at issue.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: This complete closing reply states the denied maximal-hospitality premise, offers the mudroom contrast, and restates the conditional surprise claim.
moves.attributionRationale: It is Schieber’s formal closing.
moves.importanceRationale: It is Schieber’s final clarification of a central qualification.

burdenContact.rationale: It defends the hostility comparison against an overstated premise.

responseComponents.description: Clarifies that the argument asks for an intermediate degree of hospitality rather than human-centered maximal safety.

moves.speaker: Justin Schieber
moves.claim: Showing that theism can possibly accommodate suffering does not show that it explains the observation as well as naturalism.
moves.warrant: A comparative likelihood argument requires antecedent reason to expect unknown justifying purposes, rather than mere logical room for them.
moves.inference: The suffering evidence retains comparative force unless the theistic likelihood is positively supported.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: The final formal-debate argument reconstructs Rauser’s contextual appeal and distinguishes possible accommodation from comparative explanatory likelihood before the closing thanks.
moves.attributionRationale: It is the end of Schieber’s formal closing before the moderator resumes.
moves.importanceRationale: It is Schieber’s last answer to the skeptical-theist reply and closes the assessed exchange.

burdenContact.rationale: It states the evidential standard for the suffering comparison.

responseComponents.description: Argues that contextual possibility does not establish comparative probability.
